10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates GPT's own autoregressive generation process, producing text one token at a time, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
vocabulary = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat", "END"]

def predict_next_token_probabilities(generated_so_far, rng):
    # a genuinely simplified stand-in for GPT's own next-token prediction, already covered in this topic
    return rng.dirichlet(np.ones(len(vocabulary)))

generated_sequence = []
for step in range(6):  # already covered as autoregressive generation in this topic
    probabilities = predict_next_token_probabilities(generated_sequence, rng)
    next_token_index = np.argmax(probabilities)
    next_token = vocabulary[next_token_index]
    if next_token == "END":
        break
    generated_sequence.append(next_token)
    print(f"Step {step + 1}: generated '{next_token}', sequence so far: {' '.join(generated_sequence)}")

print(f"\nFinal generated text: {' '.join(generated_sequence)}")
print("Each new word genuinely depended on everything already generated, already covered as autoregressive generation in this topic")

Unlike BERT's masking objective, GPT trains purely on generative, next-token prediction.
This simple objective requires no separate labeling, making it remarkably easy to scale.
At sufficient scale, GPT models learned few-shot learning, performing new tasks from prompt examples.
GPT generates text autoregressively, each new word depending on everything already generated.
Successive GPT versions grew dramatically in scale, each building on the one before it.
Large GPT models are often used directly through prompting, without fine-tuning at all.
It delivers strong, flexible, open-ended text generation.
